beats.narration_text: Capacity fifty. Item A weighs ten and pays sixty. B weighs twenty and pays one hundred. C weighs thirty and pays one hundred twenty. Value per pound says A first, then B. The bag is full at weight thirty with value one hundred sixty, and C no longer fits.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE INSTANCE 1 · Item cards and bag animate density-greedy A then B; C is rejected by remaining capacity.

beats.narration_text: But remove those choices and try B with C. Their weights make exactly fifty, and their values make two hundred twenty. The locally densest item blocked the globally best pair. Greedy was not unlucky; zero-one knapsack has no greedy-choice property because items are indivisible.

beats.narration_text: So ask smaller questions in a strict order. With only item A, capacities below ten stay zero; ten through twenty become sixty. Add B: capacity twenty compares keeping sixty with taking B from the empty zero-capacity answer. One hundred wins. Every cell is written once.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE INSTANCE 2 · Split stage: item cards left, immutable rows for capacities 0–20 right.

beats.narration_text: Now extend the same questions through capacity fifty. The B row reaches one hundred sixty at capacity thirty. Nothing in that finished row changes when C arrives; C gets a new row, built only from those smaller, permanent answers.
beats.tts_normalized_text: Now extend the same questions through capacity fifty. The B row reaches one hundred sixty at capacity thirty. Nothing in that finished row changes when C arrives; C gets a new row, built only from those smaller, permanent answers.
beats.new_visual_element: ROLE INSTANCE 2 · Full layer-indexed grid fills left-to-right; old ink remains untouched.

beats.narration_text: Here is the decisive cell: item C, capacity fifty. Keep the previous answer, one hundred sixty; or take C's one hundred twenty plus the best answer at remaining capacity twenty. Commit before it moves. That earlier answer is one hundred. Take gives two hundred twenty. It wins.

beats.new_visual_element: ROLE PREDICT · Held take/skip fork drives both the bag and cell (C,50), then lands 220.

beats.narration_text: Now the structure has earned its name. A cell means the best value using only the first i items at capacity w. These subproblems have an ordering: fewer items and smaller capacities come first. They also have permanence: once that exact question is solved, its answer never changes as the problem grows. Each cell is solved exactly once. A rolling row may reuse storage, but it never re-solves an answer.

beats.narration_text: The motion becomes one recurrence: the new cell is the larger of skipping the item, or taking its value plus the previous row at the remaining capacity.

beats.narration_text: At item C and capacity fifty, skip is one hundred sixty. Take is the capacity-twenty answer, one hundred, plus C's one hundred twenty. Max chooses two hundred twenty, while the bag changes to B plus C.

beats.narration_text: Every candidate comes from an earlier row, and every finished answer stays finished. That is ordering plus permanence. Now back to the bag.

beats.narration_text: The original mystery resolves on the same three items. Density-greedy returns A plus B, value one hundred sixty. Dynamic programming returns B plus C, value two hundred twenty. The table has n times W cells and constant work per cell, so this implementation takes order n W time and order n W space.

beats.narration_text: The verdict. Density-greedy loses because indivisible items do not offer a greedy-choice property. Knapsack earns dynamic programming through ordered optimal substructure and permanence. Every item-capacity question is solved once. At the decisive cell, skip gives one hundred sixty; take gives two hundred twenty.
